tts_summary:
Here's what you need to know heading into the week. This is an earnings-focused note — no big macro calls, no Fed commentary — just a deep look at the two most important tech reports of the week: SpaceX on Tuesday after the close and Meta on Wednesday after the close.

Let's start with SpaceX. Despite the recent bout of AI anxiety, sentiment heading into the print is constructive. The reason isn't Starship or Starlink — it's terrestrial data centers. SpaceX has quietly morphed into a quasi-neocloud over the last couple of quarters, leveraging its ability to build data centers faster than anyone else to lock in premium compute rates with partners like Google and Anthropic. For the quarter, the Street wants to see revenue of twelve point eight eight billion, EBITDA around six point six billion, capex of roughly nineteen point six billion, and free cash flow of negative eleven point six billion. But the numbers themselves will take a back seat to five key topics management needs to address: compute capacity goals — Musk has talked about two gigawatts of capacity by end of twenty-six and ten gigawatts by end of twenty-seven — a one hundred billion dollar ARR target by year end, an update on new compute contracts beyond Google and Anthropic, the Starlink Mobile competitive threat against the major carriers, and the ever-present Tesla merger speculation which has heated up again following the Roadster unveil.

Now to Meta — and the word here is bullish. Sentiment is extremely positive going in. The core advertising business is humming, and the Muse personal AI agent along with the Muse Wonder and Wonder Full model family have pushed Meta right to the frontier of the AI narrative. That's the good news. The complicated part is the spending. For the quarter, the Street is modeling revenue up twenty-three and a half percent to sixty-three point three billion, daily active people up three and a half percent to three point six six billion, and capex up a staggering one hundred and seventeen percent to forty-one billion dollars. That level of capex pushes free cash flow deeply negative — negative nine point two billion just for this quarter. For full-year twenty-twenty-six the consensus is negative seven point three billion in free cash flow, and twenty-twenty-seven looks even worse at negative thirty-three billion. Positive free cash flow isn't expected to return until twenty-twenty-nine. On top of that, Meta will book a ten billion dollar charge in the quarter from a settlement with state attorneys general, which will skew the headline earnings and operating income figures. There's also chatter that the company could revisit plans to sell a large slug of stock to shore up the balance sheet — shares are up significantly since those rumors surfaced, which may make management more inclined to act.

Bottom line: both prints carry high expectations. SpaceX needs to deliver on compute ambitions and ARR trajectory. Meta needs to justify an almost incomprehensible level of capital spending with a credible path to monetizing its AI product suite. These are the two events that will define the tone for tech the rest of the month. Stay sharp.
